transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-11-09
Time: 08:00 PT / 16:00 UTC
Duration: 52 minutes (recorded)
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Diego Alvarez (Redwood SE), Nina Patel (Stratum Head of ML), Omar Reyes (Stratum Platform Eng), Claire Zhou (Stratum FinOps)

Summary (auto):
Quick cost-econ discovery focused on per-token host pricing versus reserved/dedicated capacity, batching and KV cache levers, and residency requirements (VPC). Customer wants a short pilot to compare hosted and dedicated unit economics for an internal Q&A assistant (average prompt 250 tokens, expected 1.2M requests/month). Security and KMS integration are gating items.

Topics:
- Baseline per-token math (hosted)
- Batching impact on latency and unit cost
- KV/prefix cache for sessioned chat vs stateless Q&A
- Dedicated capacity sizing and cost predictability
- VPC/private deployment constraints and KMS/audit needs
- Pilot scope and next steps

--- Transcript ---
[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick roll call?
[00:07] Nina: Nina here. Morning from London.
[00:10] Omar: Omar, SF.
[00:12] Claire: Claire, finance.
[00:14] Diego: Diego from Redwood, SE.
[00:16] Maya: Cool. We're here to run through cost levers, batching, caching, and the hosting mix—hosted vs dedicated vs private—understand constraints and, uh, scope a pilot. Is that right Nina?
[00:28] Nina: Yeah that's right. We built a proof-of-concept with a small model but now looking at production economics. Big questions: what's the per-request cost if we use hosted, how much savings do we get from batching and KV cache, and whether dedicated makes sense given our traffic shape. Also security — VPC and KMS — is a must.
[00:44] Maya: Great. Diego, can you sketch the typical levers?
[00:47] Diego: Sure. So high level: per-token hosted price is straightforward — it's tokens * unit price. But you get inefficiencies if you're calling small prompts all the time. Batching reduces per-token overhead because we amortize kernel and scheduling cost across multiple requests, and prefix/KV cache helps for sessioned traffic where we can avoid re-computing common prefixes.
[01:12] Omar: Quick question — our assistant is mostly single-turn Q&A, average prompt plus response around 250 tokens, peaks during 9–11am. Will cache help?
[01:22] Diego: For single-turn it's less impactful than chat. Cache helps if many requests share context or repeated system prompts. For pure unique Q&A, batching + quantization are the bigger levers.
[01:34] Claire: Can you ballpark numbers? If we have 1.2 million requests per month at 250 tokens, what does hosted look like vs dedicated?
[01:44] Diego: I'll do a rough cal. 1.2M * 250 = 300M tokens in. If average response is 250 tokens out, that's 600M tokens — total 600M tokens/month. Hosted per-token price we typically show in examples — say $0.000006 per token (example), that would be about $3,600 / month. But that's a simplified number, doesn't account for transforms, streaming overhead, or small-request inefficiencies.
[02:12] Nina: Wait, that seems low. Our internal estimates were more like $14k. Are we missing something?
[02:19] Maya: Good call — the nominal per-token price varies by model and architecture (decoder-only vs chat models), and there's also request-level overhead and minimums. Diego?
[02:29] Diego: Right — also hosted examples for larger models or higher SLOs go up. If you use a larger quantized variant or require P95 latency of <200ms, the cost is higher. There's also inference infrastructure like concurrency and minimum request charges on certain plans. Sometimes teams see 3–4x the naive per-token calc. So your $14k range isn't implausible.
[02:56] Omar: So batching is about grouping requests; but our traffic is spiky. How does Redwood do bursty windows?
[03:03] Diego: We support autoscaling on Dedicated and elastic capacity on Hosted. For bursts, you can use a mix: Dedicated baseline pool with hosted overflow. Our routing supports fallback to cheaper model variants as well. That way you don't over-provision for peak.
[03:18] Claire: From finance perspective we like predictability. How predictable is Dedicated?
[03:22] Diego: Dedicated gives you reserved GPU pools. You pay for capacity (monthly/annual), which smooths costs and gives predictable throughput. We can model unit cost on top of the commit to give effective per-token numbers.
[03:34] Nina: We have regulatory constraints — all inference must run in our VPC or on-prem for PII workflows. Can Redwood support a private deployment with KMS HSM?
[03:44] Maya: Yes — Redwood Private supports customer-managed VPC and KMS/HSM integrations. There are some additional operational lead times and licensing; Diego can outline the steps.
[03:53] Diego: For VPC we deliver a private control plane and you manage networking. KMS integration is supported — you can bring your keys. Audit logs and RBAC are available — but keep in mind that private deployments may limit our ability to do instant autoscaling unless you provision burst capacity.
[04:11] Omar: Okay. Pilot idea — run two 48-hour benchmarks: hosted baseline and a dedicated small pool, both using our prompt set. Compare cost per effective response with batching and with cache on/off. Feasible?
[04:22] Diego: Totally. We'll provide a runbook: the benchmark will measure tokens in/out, latency percentiles, and GPU utilization. For dedicated we'll recommend a configuration (e.g., 4x A100-s or smaller depending on model).
[04:33] Claire: Who owns the billing for the pilot? Do you charge or provide credits?
[04:36] Maya: For most pilots we provide subsidized credits for hosted runs and can set up a time-boxed dedicated evaluation that can be trialed under a short-term commitment. We'll put the options in the pricing worksheet.
[04:47] Nina: A detail on batching — how does batching affect tail latency? Our SLAs require p95 < 300ms for our primary customer flows. Batching helps average cost but may hurt tail.
[04:58] Diego: Correct. Continuous batching is workload-aware: it balances latency SLOs with batch size. You can set per-route latency targets and max batching window. For p95 <300ms, we might limit batching window to 20–30ms and get modest batching gains, maybe 10–25% depending on concurrency. If you allow a higher tail, batching gives more benefit.
[05:20] Omar: And quantization — how big is the delta? We've heard 4-bit quantization cuts cost 2–3x but may degrade quality.
[05:28] Diego: Quantization (4-bit/8-bit) often reduces GPU memory and increases throughput, giving 2–3x token cost improvements for throughput-bound workloads. But quality/regression risk depends on model and accuracy sensitivity. We recommend running a small eval suite against your prompt set during the pilot. We'll suggest quant + calibration points.
[05:45] Nina: On cache: our users re-ask the same product spec questions a lot. Maybe that helps — how do you measure KV cache hit rate?
[05:52] Diego: We'll instrument cache hit/miss rate per route. If you see >20% repetitiveness on prefixes, caching can reduce compute significantly. For stateless Q&A it's less, but for product FAQ it's often meaningful.
[06:05] Claire: Any hidden costs — data egress, logging retention, tracing?
[06:09] Maya: Good question. Data egress is charged at cloud network rates if cross-region; audit log retention beyond the standard window may be an add-on. We'll itemize those in the worksheet.
[06:20] Nina: Regarding security docs — we need SOC2, pen test reports, and KMS integration docs before procurement. Can you send those?
[06:27] Maya: Yes, we'll attach the SOC2 report and a private deployment security brief. Diego, I'll ping you to assemble the KMS runbook.
[06:35] Diego: Yep. Also note for private deployment there's a verification window for KMS rotation testing — plan ~2–3 weeks for full integration testing.
[06:44] Omar: One more — do you have recommendations on model choices? We run a 7B-ish base now but it's slow on some inputs.
[06:52] Diego: Model choice depends on quality needs. For high throughput you can use a quantized 7B or smaller dense models or use a 13B lightly quantized if quality requires. We'll include model performance profiles in the pilot doc. Some teams use a smaller model for common questions and route to larger models only when confidence is low to save cost.
[07:11] Nina: That routing idea is interesting — A/B style. Is that supported out of the box?
[07:15] Maya: Yes, Redwood Console supports routing policies and fallbacks; e.g., low-cost model first, fallback to higher-quality on low confidence or rate-limit events.
[07:24] Claire: Procurement cycles — if the pilot shows dedicated is better cost-wise, what commitment terms are typical?
[07:31] Maya: We do monthly and annual reserved plans. Small teams often start with a monthly reserved pool to validate and then move to an annual commit for discounts once steady-state is proven. We'll outline typical discount bands in the pricing worksheet.
[07:44] Nina: Ok timeline — we want results before end of month. Is that realistic?
[07:49] Diego: Pilot can run in two weeks if we get the prompt set and traffic profile this week. 48-hour runs plus 3–4 days for analysis. So yes, end-of-month is feasible if we move fast.
[07:59] Maya: Let's capture next steps.
[08:02] Nina: I'll drop the sample prompt set and the 7-day traffic histogram into the shared folder by tomorrow EOD.
[08:08] Claire: I'll confirm budget lanes and commit window by next Tuesday.
[08:11] Maya: We'll send the pricing worksheet, SOC2/KMS docs, and a pilot runbook. Diego will prepare the recommended dedicated config.
[08:18] Omar: One small nit — our infra team wants SSHless deployment patterns; is installing the private agent painful?
[08:24] Diego: Private agent is containerized and can be deployed via Helm or a straight Docker compose for air-gapped. We'll include a minimal ops checklist.
[08:31] Nina: Any red flags?
[08:33] Diego: Just timing for private KMS integration and network egress if cross-region. Otherwise the plan looks standard.
[08:39] Maya: Alright let's do a quick recap of action items and owners.
[08:42] Diego: Recap: Maya sends pricing & security docs; Diego prep runbook + config; Nina shares prompts + traffic; Claire confirms budget; Stratum to pick pilot start date once prompts are shared.
[08:54] Claire: Sounds good.
[08:56] Nina: Thanks, talk soon.
[08:58] Maya: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up with calendar invites and artifacts.

(End recording)
